content: The term DMFT refers to the number of decayed, missing, or filled teeth, which is a common measure used in dental health studies. MD stands for mean difference, OR for odds ratio, and SD for standard deviation. These statistical terms are frequently used in research to analyze and interpret data. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued guidelines on sugar intake for adults and children, emphasizing the importance of reducing free sugar consumption to less than 5% of total energy intake. This recommendation is based on evidence suggesting that lower sugar intake is associated with reduced dental caries and other health benefits. The evidence supporting this recommendation was assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluations) framework. The quality of evidence for the effect of reducing free sugar intake to below 5% of total energy intake was rated as very low. This rating was due to several limitations, including the inability to conduct meta-analyses because of variability in outcome measures and the ecological nature of the studies, which precluded linking individual sugar consumption to specific health outcomes. Three national studies were reviewed, comparing dental caries levels with per capita sugar availability data. These studies consistently found higher levels of dental caries in populations with higher sugar intake. However, the ecological design of these studies made it impossible to confirm causality at the individual level. As a result, the evidence was downgraded to very low quality. The studies focused on the permanent dentition of children, but the findings were not downgraded for indirectness because the etiology of dental caries is similar in both children and adults. While primary teeth are more susceptible to demineralization due to their softer enamel, the cumulative effects of dental caries over time are relevant to all age groups. The studies were conducted in populations with low fluoride exposure, but the relationship between sugar intake and dental caries persists even in populations with adequate fluoride exposure. One study by Okuyama observed a decrease in dental caries when sugar availability was reduced from 15 kg per person per year to less than 10 kg per person per year. However, dental caries did not completely disappear, indicating that other factors also contribute to caries development. The GRADE process, typically used for controlled trials and cohort studies, was applied to the best available evidence, which in this case came from ecological studies. These studies lacked adjustments for confounding factors and did not provide individual-level data, limiting the ability to assess causality. Consequently, the evidence was conservatively rated as very low. The WHO guideline emphasizes the importance of reducing free sugar intake to improve oral health and reduce the risk of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) such as obesity. The recommendation places a high value on reducing the risk of NCDs and improving oral health, which are significant contributors to global mortality. Implementation of this guideline is expected to improve dietary quality and reduce healthcare costs in the long term. The recommendation is supported by moderate-quality evidence for the effect of reducing free sugar intake on body weight and dental caries in both adults and children. However, the evidence for the effect of increasing free sugar intake on body weight in children is of low quality, while the evidence for its effect on dental caries is moderate. The guideline also highlights the feasibility and cost-effectiveness of implementing interventions to reduce sugar intake. These interventions can be integrated into existing public health nutrition campaigns and programs at various levels, from global to local. Preventing NCDs through such measures is considered a best-buy approach, offering significant health benefits with minimal adverse effects. The WHO guideline development process involved a diverse group of experts and stakeholders, including members of the Nutrition Guidance Expert Advisory Group (NUGAG) and external peer reviewers. Conflicts of interest were managed transparently, with declarations made by all contributors. In summary, the WHO guideline on sugar intake aims to reduce the global burden of NCDs and improve oral health by recommending a reduction in free sugar consumption to less than 5% of total energy intake. While the evidence is limited in some areas, the potential health benefits and cost savings make this recommendation a valuable public health intervention.
